Speleomantes ambrosii, the Ambrosi cave salamander, is a fully terrestrial plethodontid endemic to the karstic regions of northwestern Italy and adjacent France. Neonates emerge from their yolk-dependent eggs at a total length of 2.3 cm [Lb = 2.3 cm], a diminutive size that reflects the species' direct-developing strategy, bypassing a free-swimming larval stage entirely. This species is highly stenothermal, with all major life-history processes measured under stable thermal conditions typical of subterranean environments. Growth begins slowly, with individuals under laboratory conditions at 12 °C [T = 12 °C] exhibiting an average daily increase in total length of 0.0056 centimeters per day  during the earliest post-hatching interval, a rate that underscores the low metabolic demands of a sit-and-wait forager navigating a resource-poor habitat. An important developmental milestone is the age at birth, defined as the time from oviposition to eclosion of the jelly-coated egg; at a constant temperature of 12 °C, this embryonated egg phase lasts 305 days [ab = 305 days], consistent with the prolonged incubation typical of many plethodontids inhabiting cool, thermally stable microclimates at a temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C].

Sexual maturation in this species is notably protracted relative to its small body size. Under the same thermal conditions maintaining a temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the time since birth at puberty averages approximately 1277 days [tp = approximately 1277 days], a period spent as a growing terrestrial juvenile incrementally acquiring the structural size required for gonad maturation. Body lengths at the onset of reproductive maturity exhibit clear sexual dimorphism; females attain puberty when their total length reaches 9.45 cm [Lp = 9.45 cm], while males become reproductively mature at a slightly smaller size of 8.14 cm [Lp = 8.14 cm]. This pattern is common among salamanders, where the larger investment in oogenesis constrains females to a greater size threshold before the initiation of reproductive activity. The relatively slow pre-reproductive growth phase in Speleomantes ambrosii is interpreted as a risk-averse life-history strategy, trading rapid development for longevity and consistent annual reproductive output in a stable but low-energy trophic environment.

Reproductive output in Ambrosi cave salamanders is modest but consistent, reflecting their energetically conservative lifestyle. Females produce a single clutch of 10 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 10 eggs per clutch], depositing them in damp crevices where the yolk-laden eggs develop without any aquatic stage. The maximum number of clutches produced per year is one [F_R_i = clutches produced per year is one], a frequency tightly linked to the protracted developmental period of the embryos. This combination of fecundity and frequency results in a modest annual reproductive rate, constrained by the long embryogenesis that monopolizes maternal resources for nearly the entire year. At the conclusion of the egg phase, and having been incubated at 12 °C [T = 12 °C], each hatching emerges with a wet weight at birth of 0.0871 grams [Wwb = 0.0871 grams], a value derived from the spherical egg diameter of between 5 and 6 millimeters, placing the hatchling among the smallest of European plethodontids in terms of initial mass.

Adult body size in Speleomantes ambrosii shows pronounced sexual dimorphism, a common feature among salamanders where females achieve larger asymptotes to accommodate egg production. The ultimate total length for females reaches 12.3 cm [Li = 12.3 cm], whereas males attain a smaller maximum total length of 11.6 cm [Li = 11.6 cm], a divergence that likely reflects differential selective pressures on body size for fecundity versus mate-searching ability. Correlated with this length dimorphism, the ultimate wet weight, obtained by scaling from juvenile dimensions, is approximately 13.3 grams [Wwi = approximately 13.3 grams] for a typical adult. This species is among the largest of the European cave salamanders, with a robust, moderately built body adapted for navigating narrow fissures. Longevity records, observed in captive colonies maintained at 12 °C [T = 12 °C], indicate a remarkable maximum lifespan of 17 years [am = 17 years], an exceptional duration for a small-bodied amphibian that is a testament to its exceptionally slow pace of life—a life-history syndrome characterized by delayed maturation, low fecundity, and a long reproductive window in an environment devoid of seasonal extremes.

The extraordinary longevity and slow maturation of Speleomantes ambrosii place it as an extreme example of a life-history strategy convergent with other troglophilic ectotherms. Revisiting the timing of female puberty, the time since birth at puberty of 1277 days [tp = 1277 days] required to attain a total length of 9.45 cm [Lp = 9.45 cm] is a slow progression that delays entry into the breeding population and imposes a high pre-reproductive survivorship requirement for population persistence. at a temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C]The species' pace of life is further illustrated by its modest daily elongation rate of 0.0056 cm per day  at 12 °C [T = 12 °C], a value that remains among the slowest recorded for any urodele. Among the Plethodontidae, such slow growth and late maturation are typically associated with stable, resource-limited subterranean environments, where a K-selected strategy maximizes lifetime fitness through iteroparity rather than high annual output. Clutch production is an annual event, with females once again depositing between 6 and 14 eggs [Ri = annual event, with females once again depositing between 6 and 14 eggs]. With a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], the lifetime reproductive output of an individual that lives the full 17 years [am = 17 years] is both limited and highly iteroparous, with each reproductive event representing a significant physiological investment in a handful of large, well-yolked offspring that will take 305 days [ab = 305 days] to complete embryogenesis at 12 °C [T = 12 °C]. This constellation of traits makes S. ambrosii a textbook example of a K-selected amphibian in a stable, resource-limited subterranean ecosystem.
